newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China gathers caucus to choose Hong Kong leader.
newsitem.headline: China gathers caucus to choose Hong Kong leader.

text.p: China declared the birth of democracy in Hong Kong on Friday when it inaugurated a carefully chosen caucus to choose the man who will lead the territory when the British colony reverts to China next year.
Pro-democracy activists staging noisy protests scuffled with police when China's foreign minister Qian Qichen arrived to open the meeting held in Hong Kong.

"For the past 150 years, the governors appointed by Britain numbered more than 20-odd but did they ever consult the people of Hong Kong? Of course not," Qian told the assembled panel in his opening address.
"The process of setting up the Selection Committee is the real beginning of democracy in Hong Kong and not the end of democracy in Hong Kong as some people have said," he said.
The Selection Committee members, all of them Hong Kong citizens, are charged with choosing a 60-member controversial appointed legislature as well as the future Chief Executive.
Four men have emerged as frontrunners to fill colonial governor Chris Patten's shoes when the when the British furl their flag and depart at midnight on June 30, 1997.

Two are wealthy businessmen -- Tung Chee-hwa, 59, and Peter Woo, at 50, the youngest contender. Two are former judges -- Simon Li, at 74 the oldest candidate and Ti Liang Yang, 67, Hong Kong's former Chief Justice.
Qian said the candidate had not been preordained.

Outside, pro-democracy activists brandished posters of jailed Chinese dissidents and banners condemning China's plan for an appointed legislature. Many of them spent the night outside the building staging a protest fast.
"Free Wang Dan, release Wei Jingsheng, oppose the provisional legislature," the small but noisy group of demonstrators chanted as delegates arrived in buses.

The scuffles broke out when police bundled the protesters away from the entrance before Qian, making his first official visit to the colony, arrived at Hong Kong's Convention Centre, venue for next year's handover ceremony.
Hong Kong's pro-democracy lobby has boycotted the selection process which they have branded as undemocratic and have campaigned against the provisional legislature.
"The provisional legisalature is a great step backwards for democracy," one banner said.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind warned China on Thursday its plans for a provisional legislature risked creating "confusion and uncertainty" in Hong Kong.

"China would have to explain to Hong Kong and the world why they had chosen to replace a body for which more than a million Hong Kong people voted by one chosen by a handpicked electorate of only 400," he told a parliamentary debate on Hong Kong in London.
China was infuriated by electoral reforms spearheaded by the British in the early 1990s and vowed to dissolve the chamber.
The Selection Committee will hold a first round of voting on Friday. It meets again on December 11 to pick the Chief Executive.
